title: Electricity and Magnetism
lines: Electricity and magnetism is the second big physics topic in USAT. Expect Coulomb's law and field questions, capacitors in series and parallel, resistor networks, EMF and internal resistance, force on a current or a moving charge, Faraday's and Lenz's laws, transformers and a few AC ideas. Learn the units as well as the formulas: several questions simply ask for the SI unit of a quantity.
## Electrostatics
- Coulomb's law: F = kq₁q₂/r², with k = 1/4πε₀ ≈ 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻². In a medium of relative permittivity ε(r) the force falls to F/ε(r).
- Electric field E = F/q (N/C, the same as V/m). For a point charge E = kq/r²; between parallel plates E = V/d.
- Electric potential V = kq/r is a scalar, so potentials from several charges simply add with their signs. Work to move charge q through a p.d. V is W = qV.
- 1 electronvolt (eV) = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, the energy an electron gains through 1 V.
- Gauss's law: the total flux through a closed surface = (charge enclosed)/ε₀. The field inside a charged hollow conductor is zero.
## Capacitors
- C = Q/V (farad). Parallel plates: C = ε(r)ε₀A/d, so a dielectric raises C.
- Energy stored: ½CV² = ½QV = Q²/2C.
- Parallel: C = C₁ + C₂ (same V). Series: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ (same Q).
- An RC circuit has time constant RC: in that time a capacitor charges to about 63 % of its final charge.
! Capacitors combine the opposite way to resistors: series capacitors give a smaller total.
## Current electricity
- Current I = Q/t (ampere). Ohm's law V = IR holds for a metal at constant temperature.
- Resistance R = ρL/A; resistivity ρ depends on the material and temperature, not on the wire's shape. Stretching a wire to n times its length (volume fixed) multiplies R by n².
- Series: R = R₁ + R₂ + … Parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + … n equal resistors R in parallel give R/n.
> Example 1. Three 6 Ω resistors are available. Find the total resistance when all three are in parallel, and when two in parallel are joined in series with the third.
> All in parallel: 6 ÷ 3 = 2 Ω. Two in parallel give 3 Ω; adding 6 Ω in series gives 9 Ω.
- Metals' resistance rises with temperature; semiconductors' and thermistors' falls.
- Power P = VI = I²R = V²/R. Energy = Pt, often in kWh.
- A cell of EMF E and internal resistance r drives I = E/(R + r). Terminal p.d. V = E − Ir; on open circuit V = E.
- Kirchhoff's first rule: currents into a junction = currents out (charge conserved). Second rule: in any closed loop, sum of EMFs = sum of IR drops (energy conserved).
- Wheatstone bridge: balanced (no current in the galvanometer) when P/Q = R/S.
> Example 2. A cell of EMF 12 V and internal resistance 1 Ω is connected to a 5 Ω resistor. Find the current and the terminal p.d.
> I = E/(R + r) = 12 ÷ 6 = 2 A. V = IR = 2 × 5 = 10 V; the other 2 V is "lost" inside the cell.
## Magnetism
- Force on a current-carrying wire in a field: F = BIL sin θ. The tesla is defined from this: 1 T = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹ = 1 Wb/m².
- Force on a moving charge: F = qvB sin θ. It is always at right angles to the velocity, so it does no work and the speed stays constant.
- A charge moving at right angles to B follows a circle of radius r = mv/qB.
- Field of a long straight wire: B = μ₀I/2πr. Inside a long solenoid: B = μ₀nI, where n is turns per metre; μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m/A.
- A galvanometer becomes an ammeter with a small shunt resistance in parallel, and a voltmeter with a large resistance in series.
- Magnetic flux Φ = BA cos θ (weber), where θ is the angle between B and the normal to the area.
## Electromagnetic induction
- Faraday's law: induced EMF ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt. A rod of length L moving at speed v across a field B: ε = BLv.
- Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change that causes it. This follows from conservation of energy.
- Self-inductance: ε = −L ΔI/Δt (henry). Energy stored in an inductor = ½LI².
- AC generator: peak EMF = NBAω. Its EMF is zero when the coil's plane is at right angles to the field and greatest when the plane is parallel to it.
- Ideal transformer: V(s)/V(p) = N(s)/N(p) = I(p)/I(s). It works only on alternating current. Power is sent at high voltage so that the current, and the I²R loss, is small.
> Example 3. A transformer steps 220 V down to 11 V. Its primary has 2,000 turns. How many turns does the secondary have?
## Alternating current
- V(rms) = V₀/√2 ≈ 0.707V₀. Pakistan's 220 V mains is an rms value; its peak is about 311 V.
- Inductive reactance X(L) = 2πfL rises with frequency; capacitive reactance X(C) = 1/(2πfC) falls with it.
- In a pure inductor the current lags the voltage by 90°; in a pure capacitor it leads by 90°. Neither uses power on average.
- Series RLC resonance at f = 1/(2π√(LC)): impedance is least (Z = R) and current greatest.
> Example 4. Two point charges are 10 cm apart and repel with a force of 8 N. What is the force when they are moved to 20 cm apart?
> F ∝ 1/r². Doubling r divides F by 4, so the new force is 2 N.
! A magnetic force on a moving charge never changes its speed or kinetic energy, only its direction.
! A transformer cannot step up steady DC: with no change of flux, no EMF is induced.
! Ammeters have very low resistance and go in series; voltmeters have very high resistance and go in parallel.
## Quick check
- SI unit of magnetic flux density? (tesla)
- Two 4 μF capacitors in series: total? (2 μF)
- Frequency of AC doubled: X(L) and X(C)? (X(L) doubles, X(C) halves)
- Which law expresses conservation of energy in induction? (Lenz's law)
- EMF across a cell on open circuit? (equal to its EMF; no current, no lost volts)
